Here we are looking at the 320 subject (24 removed from VIF above 4)

If we define risk aversion as extracted subject models odds larger than 1 for the risk variable and loss aversion as lambda (-risk_beta/gain_beta) > 1 then here would be the breakdown.

plotdata <- data.h %>%
  count(risk_aversion) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         pctlabel = paste0(round(pct*100), "%"))
# plot the bars as percentages, 
# in decending order with bar labels
ggplot(plotdata, 
       aes(x = reorder(risk_aversion, -pct),
           y = pct)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", 
           fill = "indianred3", 
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pctlabel), 
            vjust = -0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), 
            vjust=-3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, breaks=seq(0,1,.10), limits=c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Risk Aversion", 
       y = "Percent", 
       title  = "Participants by risk aversion")+
  theme_classic()

plotdata <- data.h %>%
  count(loss_aversion) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         pctlabel = paste0(round(pct*100), "%"))


# plot the bars as percentages, 
# in decending order with bar labels
ggplot(plotdata, 
       aes(x = reorder(loss_aversion, -pct),
           y = pct)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", 
           fill = "indianred3", 
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pctlabel), 
            vjust = -0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), 
            vjust=-3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, breaks=seq(0,1,.10), limits=c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Loss aversion", 
       y = "Percent", 
       title  = "Participants by loss aversion") +
    theme_classic()

Dominate subjects

Dominate response blurb In any discrete choice task, some participants dominate on a single attribute; that is, they always choose the alternative with the better level of the most important (dominant) attribute, regardless of the levels of the other attributes presented in the task. There are two reasons why participants might answer in this way. First, these decisions may reflect participants true preferences, and the choices presented in the task do not include combinations of other attributes that are sufficiently attractive to induce participants to choose an alternative that does not include the better level of the dominant attribute. Alternatively, participants simply may focus on only a single attribute as a way of simplifying the task of answering the trade-off questions. In the latter case, while aligned with what we’d expect from a prospect theory, from a statistical perspective their decisions will overstate the relative actual mean importance of the dominant attribute. To control for this, we first tested for differences in dominate and non-dominate response. A dominate response was identified as a selection solely of a single treatment option at or above 80% of the total amount of trials (56 trials selected for a single option) two samples t-test showed a significant difference in dominate and non-dominate responses. Thus, we excluded subjects with dominate response from our main analysis.

Testing for difference in dominate subject effects for risk (model 1) and gain (model 2)

Individual differences
